source.title: Some open problems concerning the convergence of positive series

accepted.question_text: Given an arbitrary series with positive terms, determine a general criterion or algorithm for deciding whether it converges or diverges. Is there any universal convergence test, or any structural pattern in convergence, for positive series?

evidence.quote: Problem 1. What decides if a positive series is convergent or divergent? Is there any universal convergence test? Is there any pattern in convergence?
Problem 2. Find an algorithm to determine whether a positive series is convergent or not.

accepted.question_text: Let A be a subset of the positive integers. For an increasing function phi: N -> (0, infinity) with phi(n) -> infinity, define the phi-weighted upper density of A by dbar_phi(A) = limsup as n -> infinity of |A intersect [1, n]| / phi(n). If dbar_{n/log n}(A) > 0, must the harmonic subseries sum_{n in A} 1/n diverge? More generally, for weights phi(n) = n / ((log n)(log log n)...(the k-fold iterated logarithm of n)) when these iterated logarithms are defined, does positive phi-weighted upper density force sum_{n in A} 1/n to diverge?
accepted.context_brief: weighted-density criteria for divergent harmonic subseries

evidence.quote: Problem 3. Given an increasing function ϕ : N →(0, ∞) with limn→∞ ϕ(n) = ∞, we define the upper density of weight ϕ by the formula d¯ϕ(A) = lim sup |A ∩ [1, n]| / ϕ(n).
Does every subset A ⊂ N with d¯n/ ln n (A) > 0 generate a divergent subseries ∑_{n∈A} 1/n of the harmonic series?
What about the case of other weights n/[(ln n) (ln ln n) · · · (ln · · · ln n)]?

accepted.question_text: Let A be a set of integers such that the reciprocal series sum_{n in A} 1/n diverges. Is it true that A contains arithmetic progressions of arbitrarily large finite length? In particular, must A contain at least one arithmetic progression of length three?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 1. (P. Erdös). If the sum of reciprocals of a set A of integers diverges, then that set contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
This conjecture is still open even if one only seeks a single progression of length three.
